chapters.title: A Calcutta boy
chapters.src: Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 8 · Great Master 5.8a
lines: Before he was Vivekananda, he was Naren, a boy in Calcutta.
At twilight, his mother would read him the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
His father, Western-educated, handed him a Bible and said: if there is anything called religion, it is in this.
Two worlds, side by side, in one house.

chapters.title: A line that throbbed
chapters.src: Nivedita, The Master as I Saw Him, ch. 15
lines: Reading the Gita as a boy, a single great sentence would stop him, and throb through his brain for days and nights.
They who find pleasure and pain the same, heat and cold the same, friend and foe the same.
And Krishna's words to Arjuna on the battlefield: ill doth it befit thee, Arjuna, to yield to unmanliness.
How strong, he said.

chapters.title: 1881: the books
chapters.src: Brajendranath Seal, in Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 8 · Great Master 5.8a
lines: In eighteen eighty-one, at college in Calcutta, John Stuart Mill's Three Essays on Religion upset his boyhood faith.
A friend gave him Hume's scepticism, and Herbert Spencer's doctrine of the Unknowable.
He went on to Descartes, Spinoza, Darwin, Comte, and the Germans: Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Schopenhauer.
He even attended lectures at the Medical College, to learn how the nerves and the brain work.

chapters.title: Walled in
lines: What he learned was this. The brain and the senses react to outside stimuli, and only those changes in the mind are ever known.
What the outer world really is, the thing that causes them, stays unknown and unknowable.
Inside, it is the same. Some unknown entity makes the mind say I. It too lies beyond time and space.
Inward or outward, the mind was kept back by the impregnable wall of time and space.

chapters.title: The senses err
lines: Worse, the sense perceptions themselves are full of errors.
Look at these two lines. They are exactly the same length.
Knowing it does not help. The eye still sees one longer.
So whom should philosophy trust? The senses of ordinary people, or the rare realisations of a Buddha or a Jesus?

chapters.title: Pure Reason
chapters.src: Brajendranath Seal, in Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 8
lines: His friend Brajendranath Seal offered him a system: the sovereignty of Universal Reason.
It conquered his intellect. But his heart, he confessed, still belonged to the individual.
A pale, bloodless reason could not save him in the hour of temptation.
He wanted a flesh and blood reality. A hand to save him. A master who embodied perfection.

chapters.title: Have you seen God?
chapters.src: The Vedanta in All Its Phases (CW vol. 3)
lines: So he went from place to place in Calcutta, hearing big lectures, and asking each lecturer one question.
Have you seen God?
The man would be taken aback at the very idea.
Only one man said, I have. And I will put you in the way of seeing Him too. That was Ramakrishna.

chapters.title: Where philosophy ends
chapters.src: Great Master 5.8a · Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 8
lines: The philosopher Hamilton had written that the intellect can only hint that God exists.
It cannot reveal His nature. It comes closer and closer, and never arrives.
Where philosophy ends, Hamilton said, religion begins.
Naren loved that line, and quoted it again and again.

chapters.title: A flame in a windless place
lines: Ramakrishna gave him a prayer: O God, I do not know Thy nature. Manifest Thyself to me as Thou really art.
Naren gave up every picture of God, even the formless one with attributes.
He removed all thought, and held his mind still, like the flame of a lamp in a windless place.
At times the sense of time and body vanished. He sat like this whole nights.

chapters.title: The monk in ochre
lines: One night, after meditation, a monk in ochre appeared, filling the room with light, a water pot in his hand.
He walked toward Naren, as if to say something. Seized with fear, Naren got up and left the room.
When he came back, the monk was gone.
It may be a hallucination, he said later. But very often it comes to my mind that I saw Lord Buddha that day.

chapters.title: But not God
lines: The doubts did not end in a day. He fought every inch of the way.
But slowly a conviction grew. The gods might be false, he thought. But not God.
His intellect was not stunted to be silenced. It was taken to its height, and then beyond.
The student who read Kant would become a monk, and carry Kant's question to the West.
